issues.legal_issue: A mining lessee is liable for interest on overdue royalty when the governing rules and the terms of its mining lease provide for that liability.
material_facts: Mining lessees held leases granted under the governing mining legislation.
A rule provided for interest on royalty remaining unpaid beyond the specified payment date.
The lease deeds incorporated a term requiring interest on overdue amounts.
The lessees delayed payment of enhanced royalty.
issues.conclusion: The mining lessees were bound to pay interest to the State under both the governing rule and the lease terms.
issues.legal_principle: The rule-making power under Sections 13(1) and 13(2)(i) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, permits rules concerning the manner and timing of royalty payment and other charges; interest for delayed payment falls within that authority. The rule and corresponding lease term were valid. Unlike the tax cases India Carbon Ltd. v. State of Assam, V.V.S. Sugars v. Govt. of A.P. and Vikrant Tyres Ltd. v. First Income Tax Officer, this was not a case of rules imposing interest without support in the governing statute. A lessee who accepted and acted under a mining lease cannot avoid its terms, as recognized in Har Shankar v. Dy. Excise and Taxation Commissioner and State of Haryana v. Lal Chand.

rule.if: mining_lease_interest_dispute and overdue_royalty and rule_makes_interest_payable_on_overdue_royalty and lease_incorporates_interest_term

predicates.mining_lease_interest_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a mining lessee must pay interest to the State on delayed royalty.
predicates.overdue_royalty: The mining lessee did not pay royalty by the time fixed for payment.
predicates.rule_makes_interest_payable_on_overdue_r: A rule governing the mining lease makes interest payable on royalty that remains unpaid beyond the payment deadline.
predicates.lease_incorporates_interest_term: The lessee's mining lease includes a term requiring interest on overdue royalty.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns interest on overdue royalty under a mining lease, and both a governing rule and the lease provide for that interest, the lessee must pay it.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who delays payment of a royalty component of the price may be liable to pay interest to the seller in the absence of a legal or contractual bar.
material_facts: The royalty burden could be passed by the mining lessees to purchasers through the price of coal.
The enhanced royalty formed part of the price payable by purchasers, and purchasers withheld that amount while its payment was delayed.
The mining lessees were liable to pay interest to the State on the delayed royalty.
No prohibition in law or in the relevant contracts was identified that prevented interest being payable by purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers were liable to compensate the mining lessees with interest for the period during which the royalty component of the price remained unpaid, subject to the separate issue of the period covered by court orders.
issues.legal_principle: Section 61 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, reflects principles of equity and permits interest by way of damages; even where its terms do not directly apply, its underlying principle may guide a just determination. The royalty amount passed on to purchasers was part of the price of the mineral. Interest may also be awarded in equity absent a contrary agreement, and a party deprived of money to which it is entitled may be compensated, as stated in Executive Engineer, Dhenkanal Minor Irrigation Division v. N.C. Budharaj. The liability of the mining lessees to pay interest to the State reinforced the purchasers' liability for withholding the corresponding amount.

rule.if: consumer_interest_dispute and royalty_component_was_part_of_price and consumer_delayed_payment and seller_was_liable_for_interest_on_the_same_amount and not interest_was_barred

predicates.consumer_interest_dispute: The proceeding concerns a purchaser's liability to pay interest to a seller for delayed payment of a price component.
predicates.royalty_component_was_part_of_price: The amount corresponding to royalty was passed on to the purchaser as part of the price of the goods.
predicates.consumer_delayed_payment: The purchaser kept the relevant price amount unpaid after it was due.
predicates.seller_was_liable_for_interest_on_the_sa: The seller was liable to pay interest to another party on the corresponding delayed amount.
predicates.interest_was_barred: A law or agreement prohibited the seller from recovering interest from the purchaser.

issues.definition: A purchaser who delays payment of a price component that the seller must pay onward is liable to compensate the seller with interest unless interest is barred.

issues.legal_issue: A party that benefits from an interim order later displaced by the final decision may be required to pay interest to restore the opposing party's position.
material_facts: Interim court orders prevented recovery of the enhanced royalty from purchasers while their challenges were pending.
The purchasers retained the money during the period those orders operated.
The final decision rejected the purchasers' challenges, and the enhanced royalty was then paid.
The opposing party had been deprived of the use of money it was ultimately entitled to receive.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers were liable to pay interest for the period in which the interim orders had prevented recovery, as restitution for the benefit they obtained and the loss suffered by the opposing party.
issues.legal_principle: Restitution restores a party, so far as justice permits, to the position it would have occupied but for an order later displaced by the final decision. Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, recognizes this pre-existing principle, while the court also has inherent jurisdiction to order restitution. The principle applies where a party gains an advantage, or another suffers a loss, because of an interim order that is not sustained by the final decision; interest is a normal form of restitution. The Court relied on Zafar Khan v. Board of Revenue, Jai Berham v. Kedar Nath Marwari, Rodger v. Comptoir d'Escompte de Paris and A.A. Nadar v. S.P. Rathinasami.

rule.if: restitution_dispute_after_interim_order and interim_order_suspended_recovery and interim_order_beneficiary_retained_money and final_decision_rejected_beneficiary_claim and opposing_party_was_deprived_of_money

predicates.restitution_dispute_after_interim_order: The proceeding concerns restoring benefits obtained under an interim court order after the final decision.
predicates.interim_order_suspended_recovery: A court order temporarily prevented recovery of money from a party.
predicates.interim_order_beneficiary_retained_money: The party protected by the interim order retained money that would otherwise have been paid.
predicates.final_decision_rejected_beneficiary_clai: The final decision rejected the claim of the party that benefited from the interim order.
predicates.opposing_party_was_deprived_of_money: The opposing party was kept from money it would otherwise have received during the interim order's operation.

issues.definition: When a party retains money under an interim order that is displaced by a final decision rejecting that party's claim, and the opposing party was deprived of the money, interest may be required to restore the opposing party's position.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to increase an interest rate reduced by the lower court where the reduction is reasonable in the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The State appealed against the lower court's reduction of the interest rate sought from the mining lessees.
The litigation had continued for a long time and multiple commercial transactions had taken place.
Commercial and bank interest rates had changed substantially, and bank rates had for some time been below the rate awarded by the lower court.
The lower court considered the higher rate excessive and its reduced rate reasonable in the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the lower court's reduced rate in the exercise of its discretionary appellate jurisdiction, while making clear that this case-specific concession was not a precedent for overriding the governing rule.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court declined discretionary interference with the lower court's assessment, taking account of the prolonged litigation, intervening commercial transactions and changes in interest rates. The Court expressly confined its decision to the facts and parties before it and stated that it did not override Rule 64A of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960.

rule.if: appeal_seeks_higher_interest_rate and prolonged_litigation and commercial_interest_rates_changed and lower_court_reduced_rate_reasonably

predicates.appeal_seeks_higher_interest_rate: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to restore a higher interest rate that the lower court reduced.
predicates.prolonged_litigation: The dispute has continued for a long period before the appellate decision.
predicates.commercial_interest_rates_changed: Commercial or bank interest rates changed substantially during the period of the dispute.
predicates.lower_court_reduced_rate_reasonably: The lower court reduced the rate after finding the higher rate excessive in the circumstances.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks a higher rate after prolonged litigation, commercial interest rates have changed, and the lower court's reduction was reasonable, the appellate court may leave that reduced rate undisturbed.
